lesson.grammar_point: past continuous x past simple: was / were + -ing for an action in progress (I was reading in bed) interrupted by a short action in the past simple (when the lights went out); while + past continuous, when + past simple

listenings.text: I've had this bookshop for fifteen years, and one shelf is always empty first: thrillers and mysteries. People come in for a cookbook and leave with a thriller. Last winter, a man bought one on a Friday afternoon. On Monday morning, I was opening the door when I saw him outside. He was holding the book and smiling. He didn't say hello. He just asked, do you have the next one by the same writer? That's a page-turner. In my opinion, the best thrillers have three things: a normal start, a clue that nobody sees, and a twist at the end that changes everything.

I don't usually read scary books, but a friend gave me a thriller for my birthday. One night, I was home alone, and I was reading in bed. It was raining, and there was a big storm outside. I was reading the last chapter, the main character was walking into a dark basement, and suddenly the lights went out. The whole house was black. I wasn't scared, of course. Well, maybe a little. I didn't want to stop, so I found my phone and I finished the book with the light of the screen. I didn't sleep much that night, but I found out who did it.

People always ask me where my ideas come from. The twist in my first novel came from a train station. I was waiting for a train in Berlin, and I was feeling bored. Then I saw a woman who was carrying two identical suitcases. While I was watching her, she put one suitcase on the floor, and a man took it. That was it. Nothing happened. But I started to imagine a plot. Who was the man? What was in the suitcase? I wrote the first chapter on the train. Today, I write every clue on a small card, so I know exactly where each one is in the story.

reading.rtitle: A Page-Turner: Why We Can’t Put Thrillers Down
paras: It was almost midnight. You were reading in bed, and you were planning to stop at the end of the chapter. Then the main character opened a door, and you turned the page. And another one. If this sounds familiar, you know what a page-turner is. Thrillers are among the best-selling books in the world, and readers often say the same thing: “I was going to sleep early, but I couldn’t stop.”

Most thrillers start on a normal day. The main character is doing something ordinary — cleaning an old house, working late at the office, traveling by train — when she finds something strange: a letter, a photo, a manuscript in a drawer. From that moment, she suspects everyone, and so do we. A good writer hides a clue on almost every page, but we only see it later, when it is too late.

Then comes the twist. Just when we think we know the truth, we find out that the story was something else. Some people think thrillers are scary, but most of them are not horror: there are no monsters, only people and their secrets. Psychologists say that we enjoy the fear because we are safe on the sofa. And when a thriller becomes a film, the old question comes back: was the book better? Most readers say yes.
